1	# Task 13: Coral reef underwater with camera orbit
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite. It must render one full-viewport canvas with id #app. The scene is a shallow tropical coral reef seen underwater. Show a sandy seabed with rippled patterns, several coral formations in different shapes (branching, rounded brain, fan or tube shapes) and colours, and swaying seaweed or anemones. A school of at least 30 small fish should swim in a loose group, plus 2 or more larger solitary fish on their own paths. Sunlight should enter from above, with a bluish-green water tint, depth-based colour fade, and drifting caustic-like light patterns on the sand. A few bubbles or particles should rise slowly. The camera orbits slowly around the reef centre at a gentle height, with a slight bob, and no user input is needed. Do not rely on external downloads; build everything from simple procedural shapes.

content.thinking: I'm not sure of the default value for this flag, so I should check what A3D_QR_CAMERA defaults to.

I'm planning to call setPose each frame with position and target (and fov), defaulting this on, and guarding against a missing camera. I'm also checking whether a static pose needs a "cut" flag versus smooth lookAt transition.

If setPose doesn't take effect, the camera would just stay static, which is tolerable, though adding orbit auto-rotate as fallback could conflict with this approach, so I'll skip it and instead double-check CameraController.setPose directly.

Now I'm designing the underwater scene itself: a bluish-green tinted background with fog for depth fade, a directional sunlight casting shadows tinted blue-green onto the sand and coral, and a custom shader on the sand that animates a caustic light pattern by combining ambient light with the caustic effect in the fragment calculation.

I'm planning to disable built-in fog and compute it manually in the shader using distance to the camera, and I'll build the sand as a CPU heightfield geometry with analytic ripple displacement, deriving normals from the same ripple function for lighting, caustics, and fog all within the fragment shader. I need to be careful with the GLSL syntax (WebGL2 ES 3.00 conventions) since a shader compile failure would make the sand invisible.

I'm also deciding to use my own time uniform rather than relying on an assumed prelude uniform, and avoiding naming collisions with built-in variables. Since I have no way to preview the render and tone mapping might desaturate colors, I'll tune brightness and saturation conservatively but a bit higher than normal to compensate, and set up exponential fog with a density calibrated to the scene's roughly 30-unit scale.

I'm picking a teal-toned fog and background color for an underwater feel, and matching the fog falloff approximation in my custom shader even though the exact exponent convention might not perfectly match built-in fog. For lighting, I'm setting up a directional light from above in a pale aqua tone with shadows, a hemisphere light with sky/ground teal tones, and a subtle neutral environment light to round out the ambiance.

Since the sand uses a custom unlit shader, real shadows won't land on it, so I'm considering faking occlusion near coral bases directly in the shader by baking coral positions as literals and computing a cheap multiplicative darkening term based on distance to each coral.

For god rays, I'm thinking of adding a handful of thin translucent cones or cylinders with low-opacity emissive material to simulate light shafts, and I need to check whether the material spec supports opacity and transparency blending for this to look right.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing particle shape options for the fire effect, considering a cone emitter with a narrow angle so particles drift upward naturally like a campfire.

For the fish, I'm planning to build each one from simple primitives—a slim body sphere plus a thin tail piece—and keep animation cheap by yawing the whole fish slightly rather than rigging a separate wagging tail joint, since that keeps the per-frame handle count manageable across dozens of fish.

For heading, I'm working out the rotation math: yaw about Y maps the forward +z axis to (sinψ, 0, cosψ), and pitch about X tilts it toward -y, so I can convert a velocity vector into the right Euler angles for each fish's orientation.

Given three.js applies rotations in XYZ order where pitch is applied last in world space, the math gets mismatched if I try to combine yaw and pitch independently, so I'll skip pitch entirely and just let fish bodies stay level, only rotating by yaw—vertical bobbing will be mild anyway.

For coloring, I'm planning shared material types—yellow-orange, blue, and silver—and setting up the small school as around 40 fish mostly in the yellow variant.

I'm giving the fish materials slight roughness and a touch of emissive color so they stay visible in dim, foggy water. For movement, I'm setting up a lightweight boids-style system where each fish follows a moving school center along a Lissajous path near the reef, then adds its own oscillating offset with unique phase and frequency, with heading computed from the finite-difference direction of motion.

For the larger fish, I'm giving each one an independent elliptical loop path with its own radius, height, and speed, using the same position-function-plus-heading-via-derivative approach. I'm also sizing the scene—reef radius, camera orbit distance and height, field of view—and tuning fog density so the sand extends far into the distance while fading smoothly into the background color.

For the sand, I'm keeping vertex displacement to large-scale dunes only, and handling the fine ripple detail analytically in the fragment shader using a sine-based height field, deriving the shading normal from the gradient of that ripple function combined with the dune's analytic normal.

I'll duplicate the dune height formula in JS so coral bases can be placed correctly at the surface height, slightly embedded for grounding.

For ripples, I'm working out the normal vector by computing the gradient of the phase function analytically, combining the directional and warping terms, then deriving the slope and surface normal from that.

I'm deciding to compute dune height and gradient analytically in both vertex and fragment shaders, using a 128x128 grid across 100 units which gives fine enough spacing relative to the dune wavelength to avoid aliasing.

Writing caustics code...

Still deriving the caustic loop math...

Taking the absolute value before the power keeps things stable, and now I'm tuning the world-space scaling of the caustic cells and how the brightness term multiplies against the sand color.

1	# Custom shaders: colour contract, chunks and NaN safety (4.1)
2	
3	`material.custom({ glsl: { vertex, fragment } })` is the escape hatch for effects the
4	built-in materials do not cover (sky, water, energy, toon ramps). It has a colour
5	contract and three failure modes that cost real time on real GPUs. Chunk names and
6	signatures: `docs/api/glsl-chunks.md`.
7	
8	## Colour contract
9	
10	- A custom shader writes **linear light**. The output stage always sRGB-encodes it,
11	  and the default ACES operator tones it down further, so a hex colour written
12	  straight to `outColor` comes out greyer than authored (a day sky read grey for
13	  exactly this reason). Post effects are not the cause: bloom, grade, vignette and
14	  fxaa leave a custom shader's colour unchanged.
15	- To show a hex colour as authored: `#include <colorspace_decode>`, wrap the colour
16	  in `a3dSrgbToLinear`, and set `output: { toneMapping: "none" }` on the app.
17	  `<colorspace_encode>` provides `a3dLinearToSrgb` for the other direction.
18	- Any other tone-mapping operator still tone-maps custom colours; tune the exposure
19	  instead of compensating in the shader.
20

Still writing coral math...

Now I'm moving on to designing tube coral clusters: 5-7 tubes per cluster with randomized offsets, heights, radii, and slight tilts for a natural look.

For each tube I'm positioning it centered along its tilt direction, scaling the cylinder body, then adding a dark flattened sphere at the top to look like a hollow opening, matching the tube's rotation so it sits flush with the rim. After the coral, I'm starting on rocks — scattering 10 large irregularly-scaled lumps.
